gloss_terse: defensive argument, proof, evidence brought forward in legal or rhetorical context
gloss_readable: This rare noun appears only in Isaiah 41:21, where God challenges the idols to 'bring forward your defenses'—your strongest arguments or proofs. The context is a courtroom scene where false gods are put on trial. Spanish translates it as 'your arguments' and English as 'your proofs,' both capturing the legal-rhetorical force. The word derives from a root meaning 'to be strong,' suggesting that these are not weak excuses but the best evidence one can muster in defense of a position.

senses.1: In Isaiah 41:21, God calls on pagan deities to present their 'defenses'—the most compelling arguments or evidence they can offer for their legitimacy. The term carries legal weight, as if in a courtroom, where the accused brings forward their strongest case. The multilingual glosses confirm this forensic sense: Spanish uses 'argumentos' (arguments), English 'proofs,' pointing to reasoned discourse meant to persuade or vindicate.

gloss_terse: restraint, control; possibly wealth (textually uncertain in Judges 18:7)
gloss_readable: This word appears in Judges 18:7 in a notoriously difficult phrase describing the people of Laish as having 'a possessor of restraint'—perhaps meaning a ruler who exercises control. However, ancient versions (Greek and Latin) understood it as 'wealth' instead, and the text may actually combine two different Hebrew words (treasure and wealth) that later scribes conflated. The range of translations reflects genuine textual uncertainty, with Spanish using 'repression' and English 'restraint' to preserve the governance sense, though the original meaning remains elusive.

senses.1: Judges 18:7 uses this term in a phrase so obscure that even ancient translators disagreed. The Hebrew tradition reads it as 'restraint' or 'control,' possibly referring to governmental authority—a ruler who keeps order. The Greek and Latin versions, however, saw 'wealth' here. Modern scholars suspect textual corruption, with some proposing the word is actually a combination of two Hebrew terms for riches that got merged in transmission. The multilingual evidence shows interpreters favoring the 'restraint' reading while acknowledging deep uncertainty.

gloss_terse: those who take insidious advantage, supplanters, deceivers who trip up another
gloss_readable: In Psalm 49:5 the psalmist laments 'the iniquity of my supplanters surrounds me'—those who scheme to take unfair advantage, to trip him up through cunning. The root evokes the imagery of the heel (aqeb), recalling how Jacob grasped Esau's heel at birth and later supplanted him. French uses 'supplanteur' (supplanter), while Spanish shifts to 'my heels' (mis talones), perhaps reading the phrase as enemies who pursue closely, nipping at one's heels. Either way, the word conveys treacherous deception aimed at gaining advantage over another.

senses.1: Psalm 49:5 speaks of 'my supplanters'—those who seek to gain advantage through deceit or trickery, as Jacob did to Esau (whose very name connects to 'heel'). The psalmist feels surrounded by their schemes. French captures this with 'supplanteur,' maintaining the sense of one who displaces another through cunning. Spanish's 'mis talones' (my heels) may reflect a different vocalization or a metaphor of enemies pursuing close behind, threatening to trip or overtake. The underlying imagery is of insidious, heel-grasping treachery.

gloss_terse: steep, hilly, rugged terrain (as opposed to level ground)
gloss_readable: Isaiah 40:4 envisions a great leveling of the landscape in preparation for God's coming: 'Let the steep ground become a plain.' This adjective describes rugged, hilly terrain—difficult to traverse—contrasted with flat plains. The root is cognate with Arabic and Ethiopic words for 'difficult mountain path' and 'hill.' Spanish renders it 'lo torcido' (the crooked), perhaps seeing moral metaphor alongside the geographical sense. The verse is about removing obstacles, whether literal mountains or metaphorical barriers, so God's glory can be revealed.

senses.1: In Isaiah 40:4, this word describes terrain that is steep or hilly, the kind of ground that makes travel arduous. The prophet declares that such rugged places will be flattened into plains when God comes. Cognate languages support this: Arabic has 'difficult mountain path,' Ethiopic 'hill.' Spanish translates 'lo torcido' (the crooked), which may blend the physical sense of winding, uneven paths with a moral sense of what is not straight. Either way, the image is of obstacles removed and rough places made smooth.

gloss_terse: cunning, craftiness, insidious trickery used to deceive
gloss_readable: In 2 Kings 10:19, Jehu acts 'with cunning'—employing deception to lure the worshipers of Baal into a trap so he can slaughter them. The word conveys insidiousness, a sly, underhanded approach to achieving one's goal. Spanish uses 'con astucia' (with cunning/cleverness), French 'avec rusé' (with craftiness). While Jehu's goal (destroying Baal worship) is presented as divinely sanctioned, the method involves deliberate deceit—pretending to honor Baal in order to gather all his worshipers in one place for execution. The term captures the morally ambiguous use of trickery for a 'righteous' end.

senses.1: In 2 Kings 10:19, Jehu uses this 'cunning' or 'craftiness' to deceive Baal worshipers into assembling for what they think will be a great sacrifice, only to be annihilated. The Hebrew root suggests insidious, underhanded scheming. Spanish 'astucia' and French 'rusé' both highlight cleverness used for deceptive ends. The narrative is morally complex: Jehu's trickery serves the elimination of idolatry (approved by the text), yet the means involve deliberate falsehood—a reminder that biblical characters sometimes accomplish divine purposes through ethically ambiguous methods.

gloss_terse: to bind, tie fast (especially of binding limbs together)
gloss_readable: This verb appears only in Genesis 22:9, the harrowing scene where Abraham 'bound Isaac' on the altar, preparing to sacrifice him. Cognate languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Syriac, Ethiopic) all share meanings related to tying, fastening, or bending limbs together. The Aramaic Targum uses the same root for binding and also for kneeling, perhaps reflecting the posture of a bound victim. The scene is one of the most emotionally intense in Scripture: a father binding his beloved son in obedience to God's command, moments before the angel intervenes.

senses.1: Genesis 22:9 records the terrible moment when Abraham 'bound' Isaac and laid him on the altar. The verb means to tie or fasten, especially limbs together—perhaps with arms behind the back or legs bent and secured. Related Semitic languages confirm this sense of tying fast. Targums also associate the root with kneeling, perhaps picturing a victim made to kneel before being bound. The single biblical occurrence is unforgettable: the father's obedience pushed to the brink, the son's vulnerability, and the binding that never culminates in sacrifice because God provides a substitute.

gloss_terse: pressure, oppression, or possibly cry for help (textually debated in Psalm 55:3)
gloss_readable: Psalm 55:3 uses this rare Aramaic-derived word, translated 'because of the pressure of the wicked' or 'oppression.' The psalmist is in distress, and this term captures the crushing weight of hostile forces. However, some scholars suggest the text should read 'cry' (tsa'aqat) instead, which would parallel the 'voice' (qol) earlier in the verse and fit the context of crying out to God. Spanish uses 'opresión,' French 'angoisse' (anguish), both conveying intense distress. Whether 'pressure' or 'cry,' the sense is of overwhelming trouble caused by enemies.

senses.1: In Psalm 55:3, this Aramaic loanword describes the 'pressure' or 'oppression' the psalmist feels from wicked adversaries. The term suggests a crushing weight, a squeezing force that causes anguish. Some scholars, noting the parallel structure with 'voice' earlier in the verse, propose emending to 'cry' (tsa'aqat), which would make better poetic sense: 'voice... cry of the wicked.' Still, the transmitted Hebrew points to 'pressure,' and the multilingual glosses ('opresión,' 'angoisse') capture the feeling of being hemmed in by hostile forces, barely able to breathe.

gloss_terse: bent out of shape, twisted, perverted (passive participle describing distortion)
gloss_readable: Habakkuk 1:4 laments that 'justice comes out perverted'—literally, bent out of shape, twisted like metal or wood forced into a crooked form. This passive participle paints a picture of something originally straight that has been deformed. The verb root means to bend or twist, found in Hebrew, Aramaic, Syriac, and Arabic with similar senses. The prophet is decrying a legal system so corrupt that what should be straight (justice) emerges crooked. Spanish uses 'pervertido,' French 'se tordre' (to twist), both evoking the image of warping or distortion.

senses.1: Habakkuk 1:4 uses this passive participle to describe justice that is 'perverted'—literally bent or twisted out of its proper shape. The root appears across Semitic languages meaning to bend, twist, or make crooked. The prophet's complaint is that the wicked surround the righteous, so justice cannot emerge straight—it comes out warped, like a piece of metal hammered into a wrong form. Spanish 'pervertido' and French 'se tordre' both capture the sense of something good (justice) being deformed into something crooked by corrupt handling.

gloss_terse: twisting, crooked (adjective); possibly the constellation Draco (the dragon/serpent)
gloss_readable: Isaiah 27:1 speaks of 'Leviathan the twisting serpent,' using this adjective to describe the mythic sea monster's sinuous, coiling form. Some scholars suggest it may also refer to the constellation Draco, the celestial dragon that twists around the northern sky. The word conveys crookedness, the winding, serpentine path of a creature that does not move in a straight line. Spanish translates 'tortuosa' (tortuous, winding), confirming the sense of something that curves and bends. In apocalyptic imagery, Leviathan represents chaos and evil that God will ultimately destroy.

senses.1: In Isaiah 27:1, this adjective describes Leviathan as 'twisting' or 'crooked,' evoking the image of a serpent coiling and winding through the sea. The Hebrew tradition preserves the sense of something that moves in curves rather than straight lines—sinuous, evasive. Some scholars see a reference to the constellation Draco, the dragon whose tail twists around the pole star. Spanish 'tortuosa' reinforces the winding, tortuous nature. In prophetic eschatology, this crooked serpent symbolizes cosmic evil that God will slay on the final day, establishing His reign over chaos.

gloss_terse: Akan, a personal name in Edom (Genesis 36:27); variant Jaakan in Chronicles
gloss_readable: Akan is a name appearing in the genealogy of Edom in Genesis 36:27, where he is listed among the sons of Ezer. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 1:42 gives the name as Jaakan, and related references speak of 'the sons of Jaakan' and 'the wells of the sons of Jaakan,' suggesting his descendants became a known clan or settlement. Greek versions transliterate it variously (Oukam, Iakan). The textual variation between Akan and Jaakan is minor, likely reflecting different pronunciations or scribal traditions. The name is Edomite, belonging to the genealogies tracing Esau's descendants.

senses.1: Akan is an Edomite name in Genesis 36:27, listed among the descendants of Seir the Horite. In the parallel genealogy at 1 Chronicles 1:42, he is called Jaakan. Elsewhere Scripture mentions 'Bene-Jaakan' (the sons of Jaakan) as a place name during Israel's wilderness wanderings. The Greek versions offer various transliterations (Oukam, Iakan, Onan), showing some fluidity in pronunciation. The variation Akan/Jaakan is typical of genealogical transmission across centuries. This Edomite figure becomes associated with a well or settlement, one of many clan ancestors who gave their names to locations.

gloss_terse: offshoot, branch, member of a family or clan stemming from a root
gloss_readable: Leviticus 25:47 uses this term in a legal context: if an Israelite becomes impoverished and sells himself to a sojourner, he may be redeemed by 'an offshoot of the sojourner's family'—literally, a branch or member stemming from the family tree. The word evokes botanical imagery, as an offshoot grows from the root of a plant. It emphasizes kinship connection, even extended or indirect. Spanish translates 'la raíz' (the root), French 'offshoot,' both pointing to the idea of family lineage extending outward. This provision allows even a distant relative of the foreign master to act as kinsman-redeemer.

senses.1: Leviticus 25:47 refers to 'an offshoot of a sojourner's family'—a member or branch of the extended clan. The term derives from the root, suggesting someone who has grown out from the family tree, perhaps a distant relative or a member of a sub-branch. The legal context is the redemption of an enslaved Israelite: even a non-direct descendant, as long as he is connected to the family, can act as redeemer. Multilingual glosses ('raíz' in Spanish, 'offshoot' in French) preserve the organic, botanical metaphor of kinship branching outward from a common root.

gloss_terse: Eqer, a personal name in the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:27)
gloss_readable: Eqer is a name mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2:27. He is listed among the sons of Jerahmeel, part of the extended Judahite clans. The name appears only this once in Scripture, and ancient Greek versions transliterate it variously (Akor, Ikar). Beyond this single reference, nothing more is known about Eqer—he is one of many names preserving the memory of early Israelite families. The genealogies in Chronicles serve to anchor post-exilic Israel in its tribal heritage, remembering even obscure figures like Eqer.

senses.1: Eqer appears in 1 Chronicles 2:27 within the genealogy of Jerahmeel, a branch of the tribe of Judah. His name is preserved but no deeds or details accompany it—he is simply one link in the chain of Judahite ancestry. Greek manuscripts render the name as Akor or Ikar, showing slight variations in pronunciation. The Chronicler's genealogies aim to reconstruct Israel's lineage after the Babylonian exile, and names like Eqer, though otherwise unknown, testify to the thoroughness with which the community remembered its roots. He is an ancestor, and that alone warrants his place in sacred history.

gloss_terse: Arad, a personal name in the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:15)
gloss_readable: This Arad is a Benjamite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:15, distinct from the more famous Canaanite city of Arad in the Negev. He appears in the genealogy of Benjamin, one of the many descendants traced through the tribe's clans. Greek versions transliterate the name variously (Orēr, Arōd, Arad), reflecting different manuscript traditions. The name itself is not explained in the text, and this individual Arad is otherwise unknown. He is one of the numerous Benjamites whose names are preserved in the Chronicler's effort to document Israel's tribal structure after the exile.

senses.1: Arad in 1 Chronicles 8:15 is a Benjamite, listed among the sons of Elpaal in the tribe's genealogy. This is not the Canaanite city of Arad, but a personal name borne by a member of Benjamin. The Greek versions show textual variation (Orēr, Arōd, Arad), suggesting some fluidity in the transmission of the name. No narrative accompanies this mention—Arad is simply part of the genealogical record that anchors Benjamin's post-exilic community to its ancestral past. The Chronicler's lists preserve the memory of families and individuals who might otherwise be forgotten.

gloss_terse: wild donkeys, untamed asses (Aramaic form used in Daniel)
gloss_readable: Daniel 5:21 recounts how Nebuchadnezzar was driven from human society and 'his dwelling was with the wild donkeys.' This Aramaic word for wild ass emphasizes the king's degradation—reduced to living like an animal, grazing with the untamed beasts of the field. The wild donkey is a symbol of freedom and wildness in biblical literature, but here it underscores the humiliation of a once-great monarch. The term is cognate with Hebrew, Syriac, and Aramaic words for the same animal. Spanish uses 'los asnos salvajes,' confirming the sense of undomesticated, free-roaming creatures of the wilderness.

senses.1: In Daniel 5:21, this Aramaic word describes the 'wild donkeys' with whom the mad king Nebuchadnezzar lived during his period of insanity. The wild donkey is a creature of the open steppe, untamed and free, and placing the king among them signifies his utter loss of human dignity and reason. Aramaic and Syriac have cognate terms for this animal, which appears elsewhere in Scripture as an image of independence and wilderness. Here, however, the emphasis is on degradation: the mighty emperor eating grass like an ox, dwelling with wild beasts, until he acknowledges the sovereignty of the God of heaven.

gloss_terse: bare places, possibly vegetation stripped by the Nile or meadows laid bare
gloss_readable: Isaiah 19:7 mentions 'bare places' by the Nile, possibly referring to areas of exposed ground where vegetation has been stripped away, or perhaps to reeds and grasses that are harvested, leaving the banks bare. The Hebrew is uncertain—the Greek translates it as 'reeds' (achei), and some scholars think the original word referred to plant life rather than empty ground. Spanish uses 'lugares desnudos' (naked/bare places). The context is a prophecy of Egypt's desolation, where the Nile's once-fertile banks will fail to produce. Whether bare soil or withered plants, the image is of loss and barrenness.

senses.1: Isaiah 19:7 speaks of 'bare places' by the Nile, in a prophecy foretelling Egypt's agricultural collapse. The term is obscure; the Greek understood it as 'reeds,' and some Hebrew manuscripts or interpretations see vegetation here. The Hebrew as transmitted suggests bareness—exposed ground, places stripped of their covering. Spanish 'lugares desnudos' captures the nakedness, the absence of what should be there. In context, this is part of a broader vision of Egypt's rivers drying up, fishermen lamenting, and the land's fertility vanishing—a reversal of Egypt's traditional abundance.

gloss_terse: wild donkey, untamed ass (likely Aramaic loanword, equivalent to Hebrew pere)
gloss_readable: Job 39:5 asks, 'Who has let the wild donkey go free?' using this term, which is likely an Aramaic loanword equivalent to the more common Hebrew 'pere.' The wild donkey is a creature of the open desert, free and untamed, symbolizing independence and the wildness of creation that owes nothing to human control. God's speech in Job 38–41 highlights animals that live outside human dominion, and the wild donkey epitomizes this: no one has domesticated it, no one feeds it, yet it thrives in the wilderness. Spanish 'onagro' (from Latin/Greek) is the technical term for wild ass, confirming the identification.

senses.1: In Job 39:5, God asks who has set 'the wild donkey' free—a rhetorical question emphasizing divine sovereignty over creation. This Aramaic-derived term denotes the same animal as Hebrew 'pere,' the untamed ass that roams the desert steppes. Targums and Syriac confirm the identification. The wild donkey in Job is an emblem of freedom: it scorns the city, ignores the driver's shout, ranges the mountains for pasture. It exists entirely outside human systems, a creature whose liberty is God's gift. Spanish 'onagro' and the technical zoological tradition preserve this identity as the Asiatic wild ass.

gloss_terse: dishonor, nakedness, shame (Aramaic cognate of Hebrew 'ervah')
gloss_readable: Ezra 4:14 uses this Aramaic word, stating 'it is not fitting for us to see the king's dishonor,' as the adversaries of the Jews write to the Persian king. The term is cognate with Hebrew 'ervah' (nakedness, shame), carrying the sense of exposure and disgrace. The context is political: the letter-writers claim loyalty to the king and say they cannot stand by while he is dishonored (presumably by the rebuilding of Jerusalem, which they portray as a threat). Spanish translates 'deshonra' (dishonor), capturing the social and political dimension of shame. The word evokes vulnerability and loss of dignity.

senses.1: In Ezra 4:14, enemies of the Jewish community write to King Artaxerxes, saying 'it is not fitting for us to see the king's dishonor.' This Aramaic term is related to Hebrew 'ervah' (nakedness, shame), conveying exposure, vulnerability, disgrace. The accusers frame their opposition to Jerusalem's rebuilding as loyalty: they cannot tolerate the king being shamed (by a potentially rebellious city). Spanish 'deshonra' rightly emphasizes honor culture—seeing the king dishonored would implicate them in betrayal. The rhetoric is self-serving, but the word reveals how nakedness/dishonor functions as a powerful social sanction.

gloss_terse: dreadful, terrible (adjective describing a fearsome ravine or gorge)
gloss_readable: Job 30:6 describes the destitute as living 'in the most dreadful of ravines,' using this adjective to convey terror and awfulness. The word may be a passive participle meaning 'feared' or 'dreaded,' applied to a landscape so harsh and frightening that it becomes the refuge only of the desperate. The term evokes not just physical danger but the eerie, fearsome quality of desolate canyons where outcasts hide. Spanish uses 'en barranco' (in the ravine), focusing on the geographical feature, while the Hebrew emphasizes the ravine's dreadfulness. Job is recounting the degradation of those who once scorned him—people reduced to dwelling in terrifying, uninhabitable places.

senses.1: Job 30:6 uses this adjective to describe ravines or gorges so dreadful that only the most desperate outcasts live there. The term likely derives from a root meaning 'to fear' or 'to dread,' making this a passive participle: 'dreaded ravines.' The context is Job's lament over those who mock him—people so degraded they dwell in frightful, desolate canyons. These are not ordinary valleys but places of terror, perhaps haunted or cursed in the ancient imagination. Spanish 'barranco' names the place, while the Hebrew stresses its fearsome character—an environment so harsh it mirrors the social abyss of its inhabitants.

gloss_terse: the Erite, collective gentilic denoting the clan descended from Eri (Numbers 26:16)
gloss_readable: Numbers 26:16 lists 'the Erite' as one of the clans of Gad, descended from Eri. The term is a gentilic (ethnic/clan adjective) used collectively with the article to denote the family group. In the wilderness census, each tribe is subdivided into clans, and this is one such subdivision within Gad. The name Eri itself is otherwise obscure, known only from this genealogical context. Greek transliterates it as Addei. The Erites are part of the tribal structure that organizes Israel's military and social life during the wilderness period and the conquest.

senses.1: In Numbers 26:16, 'the Erite' designates the clan descended from Eri, a son of Gad. This gentilic form (with the definite article) functions as a collective noun, referring to the whole family group. The wilderness census counts each tribe by its constituent clans, and the Erites are one such lineage within Gad. Nothing else is recorded about Eri or his descendants, but their inclusion in the census ensures they are recognized as a legitimate part of Israel's tribal inheritance. The Greek Addei reflects a variant pronunciation, common in genealogical transmission.

gloss_terse: clouds (possibly thick, dark clouds that obscure light)
gloss_readable: Isaiah 5:30 warns of a coming darkness: 'if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress, and the light is darkened in its clouds.' This rare noun refers to clouds, possibly the thick, heavy kind that blot out the sun. One scholar proposes emending the text to read 'through its brightness,' referring instead to the land, but the transmitted Hebrew has 'clouds.' The image is apocalyptic—light swallowed by ominous cloud cover, symbolizing judgment and gloom. Spanish uses 'por sus nubes' (by/through its clouds), maintaining the meteorological reference. The verse closes Isaiah's woe oracles with a vision of deepening doom.

senses.1: Isaiah 5:30 mentions 'clouds' that darken the light, as part of a vision of coming judgment. The noun is rare and its exact nuance debated, but it clearly refers to cloud cover—probably thick, oppressive clouds that obscure the sun. Some scholars suggest textual emendation, but the Hebrew as it stands points to atmospheric gloom: the land is in darkness and distress, and even the light is swallowed by clouds. Spanish 'sus nubes' confirms the meteorological sense. In prophetic imagery, such clouds often symbolize divine wrath or the darkness of exile and catastrophe.

gloss_terse: to be heaped up, piled up (Niphal, of water or other substances)
gloss_readable: Exodus 15:8 celebrates the miracle at the Red Sea: 'The waters were heaped up... the floods stood upright as a heap.' This Niphal verb describes water piling up vertically, defying gravity as God blows with His breath. Cognate languages (Sabean, Arabic, Aramaic, Syriac) share roots related to heaps, dams, and piles. The imagery is of water forming a wall or mound, creating a path through the sea. Spanish 'se amontonaron' (they piled up) and French 'piled up' both capture the sense of accumulation and vertical stacking. It is a miraculous reversal of water's natural flow.

senses.1: Exodus 15:8 uses this Niphal verb to describe how 'the waters were heaped up' when God parted the Red Sea. The verb conveys piling or stacking, as if the sea became a solid heap or wall. Cognates in Sabean, Arabic, and Syriac refer to dams, heaps, or embankments, confirming the sense of accumulated mass. The miracle is that fluid water behaves like solid matter, standing upright in defiance of nature. Spanish 'amontonaron' and French 'piled up' preserve the vertical, heaped imagery. This is Israel's founding deliverance—water transformed into walls by the breath of God.

gloss_terse: craftiness, cunning, shrewd wisdom used for deceptive ends
gloss_readable: Job 5:13 declares that God 'catches the wise in their own craftiness,' quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19. This noun denotes cunning or shrewdness, the clever scheming of those who think themselves too smart to be caught. The root is related to 'ormah' (craftiness) and may derive from the idea of being shrewd or prudent. The context in Job is ironic: human cleverness becomes a trap when God intervenes. Spanish 'en su astucia' (in their cunning) and the idea of 'craftiness' both convey intelligence turned toward deceptive or self-serving ends. It is wisdom without righteousness.

senses.1: Job 5:13 says God 'catches the wise in their craftiness,' using this noun to denote cunning or clever scheming. The term is related to 'ormah' (prudence, shrewdness), often with a negative connotation when it becomes mere cleverness for selfish gain. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 3:19, applying it to human wisdom that opposes God. Spanish 'astucia' captures the sense of cunning intelligence—mental agility used for deceptive purposes. The irony is that craftiness, no matter how sophisticated, becomes the snare of those who rely on it instead of fearing God.

gloss_terse: Eran, a personal name in Ephraim (Numbers 26:36); possibly textual variant of Eden
gloss_readable: Eran is listed in Numbers 26:36 as a descendant of Ephraim, ancestor of the Eranite clan. However, the Samaritan text and some manuscripts read 'Eden' instead, and the Greek has Εδεν, suggesting textual variation. The name may be a scribal variant or a genuine alternative form. Beyond this census reference, Eran is unknown. The wilderness census preserves the clan structure of Ephraim, and whether Eran or Eden is the original reading, the name represents a legitimate family line within Joseph's tribe. The Eranites are counted among Ephraim's divisions for military and land-allocation purposes.

senses.1: Eran appears in Numbers 26:36 as an Ephraimite ancestor, though the text is uncertain—the Samaritan Pentateuch and some Hebrew manuscripts read 'Eden,' and the Greek supports this. The variation likely reflects different manuscript traditions or dialectical pronunciations. Either way, Eran/Eden is the eponymous ancestor of a clan within Ephraim. Nothing else is known about him, but his name ensures his family's place in the tribal census and eventual land inheritance. The census organizes Israel for the conquest, and every clan—even those known only by a name—has a stake in the promised land.

gloss_terse: the Eranite, collective gentilic for the clan descended from Eran (Numbers 26:36)
gloss_readable: Numbers 26:36 names 'the Eranite' as the clan descended from Eran (or Eden, per variant readings) within the tribe of Ephraim. This gentilic form, with the definite article, designates the family group collectively. The Samaritan text and Greek manuscripts reflect 'Edenite' instead, consistent with the variant reading of the ancestor's name. Regardless of spelling, the Eranites are one of the Ephraimite clans counted in the wilderness census. They represent a subdivision of Joseph's prominent tribe, entitled to a portion of the land inheritance west of the Jordan.

senses.1: In Numbers 26:36, 'the Eranite' denotes the clan descended from Eran, part of the tribe of Ephraim. The term is a gentilic used collectively (with the article) to refer to the whole family group. Textual variants (Samaritan 'Edenite,' Greek Εδενει) suggest the name was transmitted with some variation, but the sense is clear: this is a recognized lineage within Ephraim. The census ensures each clan's identity and land claim. The Eranites, though otherwise unknown, are numbered among the tribes of Israel and have a place in the covenant community.

gloss_terse: the destitute, stripped, one left bare and without resources
gloss_readable: Psalm 102:17 speaks of God regarding 'the prayer of the destitute,' using this adjective (with article) as a noun for someone utterly stripped of resources and dignity. The root conveys bareness, nakedness, deprivation. In the ancient world, the destitute are those without land, family, or social standing—completely vulnerable. The psalmist, crying out from deep affliction, identifies with this class. Spanish 'el despojado' (the despoiled, stripped one) and French 'le nu' (the naked/bare one) both emphasize the stripping away of what sustains life. Yet the psalm affirms that God does not despise their prayer—hope exists even for the utterly destitute.

senses.1: Psalm 102:17 promises that the Lord 'regards the prayer of the destitute.' This adjective-turned-noun describes someone completely stripped, left bare of possessions, status, and hope—'the naked one,' in the social sense. The root is about bareness and exposure. In Israel's honor-shame culture, to be destitute is to have lost everything that gives one a place in society. Yet the psalmist proclaims that God does not turn away from such prayers. Spanish 'despojado' and French 'nu' both capture the vulnerability. This is a theology of divine attentiveness to the lowest, those the world ignores.

gloss_terse: the Aroerite, gentilic denoting someone from Aroer (1 Chronicles 11:44)
gloss_readable: First Chronicles 11:44 lists 'the Aroerite' among David's mighty warriors. This gentilic designates someone from Aroer, a place name that appears multiple times in Scripture, most commonly referring to a city on the Arnon River in Moab. The term identifies the warrior's hometown or clan origin. Greek manuscripts transliterate variously, showing some uncertainty. The mighty men of David came from diverse regions, and this Aroerite represents one such geographic and perhaps ethnic origin. He is known only by his place of origin, but his inclusion among the elite warriors honors his hometown.

senses.1: In 1 Chronicles 11:44, 'the Aroerite' is one of David's elite warriors, identified by his place of origin. Aroer is a town name appearing several times in the Hebrew Bible, most famously a Moabite city on the Arnon. The gentilic form marks the warrior's geographic or clan identity. Greek versions show slight variation in transliteration, typical of place-derived names. David's mighty men hailed from all over Israel and beyond, and this Aroerite—otherwise anonymous—earns his place in the honor roll by virtue of his valor. His hometown gains fame through his deeds.

gloss_terse: oppressor, one who extorts or defrauds by violence or injustice
gloss_readable: Jeremiah 22:3 commands, 'Do no wrong or violence to the stranger, the fatherless, or the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place, and deliver the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor.' This noun denotes one who oppresses or extorts, using power to defraud and harm the vulnerable. It is related to the more common 'osheq' (oppressor, 21:12). The context is a prophetic oracle to the king of Judah, calling for justice and protection of the weak. Spanish 'opresor' and the term 'oppressor' both convey the abuse of power. Failure to stop oppression brings divine judgment on the royal house.

senses.1: Jeremiah 22:3 calls on Judah's king to 'deliver the one robbed from the hand of the oppressor.' This noun denotes an extortioner or violent oppressor—someone who uses force or fraud to exploit others. The prophet lists the classic victims: the stranger, orphan, and widow. Protecting them from oppression is the king's sacred duty. Spanish 'opresor' rightly emphasizes the power imbalance: one who crushes those beneath him. The term is parallel to 'osheq' in 21:12, showing Jeremiah's consistent concern for social justice. Oppression is not just crime—it is covenant violation that provokes God's wrath.

gloss_terse: wrought, worked (adjective describing skilfully crafted or forged iron)
gloss_readable: Ezekiel 27:19 lists 'wrought iron' among the luxury goods traded in Tyre. This adjective describes iron that has been worked or forged—skilfully crafted, not raw ore. The text is somewhat uncertain (some scholars propose different roots or emendations), but the sense is of processed, finished metalwork suitable for commerce. Spanish 'forjado' (forged) captures the idea of iron shaped by heat and hammer. The word may derive from a root meaning to forge or work skilfully. Tyre's marketplace was renowned for exotic and high-quality merchandise, and wrought iron would have been a valuable commodity in the ancient Near East.

senses.1: Ezekiel 27:19 mentions 'wrought iron' as one of the trade goods in Tyre's bustling market. This adjective likely describes iron that has been skilfully worked or forged—finished metalwork, not crude ore. The Hebrew is somewhat uncertain, and scholars debate the root (some suggest a verb meaning to forge or work skilfully). Spanish 'forjado' supports the sense of iron crafted by smiths. In the ancient economy, worked metal—especially iron, which requires high heat and skill—was precious. Tyre's lament in Ezekiel 27 catalogues the riches of international trade, and wrought iron symbolizes human craftsmanship and commercial wealth.

gloss_terse: Ashvat, a personal name in the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:33)
gloss_readable: Ashvat appears in 1 Chronicles 7:33 within the genealogy of Asher, listed among the sons of Japhlet. The name occurs only here, and nothing is known of the individual beyond this genealogical reference. Greek versions transliterate it as Aseth or Asouath, showing minor variation. The Chronicler's genealogies preserve the tribal structure of northern Israel, including Asher, which settled along the Phoenician coast. Names like Ashvat anchor the post-exilic community to its ancestral past, maintaining continuity with the twelve tribes even after the disruptions of conquest and exile.

senses.1: Ashvat is an Asherite name in 1 Chronicles 7:33, one of the sons of Japhlet within Asher's genealogy. The name appears nowhere else in Scripture, and no deeds or details are recorded. Greek manuscripts offer variant transliterations (Aseth, Asouath), typical of genealogical transmission. The Chronicler's goal is to preserve Israel's tribal memory, especially for northern tribes like Asher that were absorbed into Assyria. By recording names like Ashvat, the genealogy insists that even the least-known descendants matter—each name is a thread in the tapestry of covenant history.

gloss_terse: Asiel, a personal name in the tribe of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:35)
gloss_readable: Asiel is named in 1 Chronicles 4:35 within the genealogy of Simeon. He is listed among the ancestors of Simeonite families, though no narrative accompanies his name. The Greek has Asiēl, a straightforward transliteration. Simeon's territory was eventually absorbed into Judah, and many Simeonites are known only through genealogical records like this. The Chronicler's preservation of names such as Asiel reflects the importance of tribal identity and inheritance, even for tribes that lost political independence. Each name represents a family line with rights, memories, and a place in the covenant community.

senses.1: Asiel appears in 1 Chronicles 4:35 as a Simeonite, part of the genealogical framework tracing the tribe's clans. No story is told about him; his name simply marks a link in the ancestral chain. Greek manuscripts transliterate as Asiēl. Simeon, the smallest tribe, was eventually integrated into Judah, and many of its members are preserved only in these lists. By including Asiel, the Chronicler affirms that every family, however obscure, has standing before God. Genealogy is not mere record-keeping—it is theology, asserting that each person's lineage matters in the story of redemption.

gloss_terse: to contend, quarrel, engage in dispute (Hithpael reflexive/reciprocal)
gloss_readable: Genesis 26:20 recounts the herdsmen of Gerar quarreling with Isaac's herdsmen over a well, saying 'The water is ours,' and Isaac named the well Esek, 'because they contended with him.' This Hithpael verb conveys reciprocal or reflexive action—contending, quarreling, engaging in conflict. The root may be related to 'clinging' in strife (cf. Arabic 'cling with love,' Syriac 'be difficult, hostile'), or to being occupied/busy (hence contention as intense engagement). Spanish 'disputaron' and the idea of contention both capture the verbal and perhaps physical struggle over water rights in the arid Negev.

senses.1: Genesis 26:20 uses this Hithpael verb to describe the conflict between Isaac's and Gerar's herdsmen: 'they contended with him' over a well. The verb suggests mutual strife, a back-and-forth quarrel. Some link the root to Arabic 'cling' (as in strife, one clings to one's claim) or to Aramaic/Hebrew 'be busy, occupied,' implying intense engagement in dispute. Spanish 'disputaron' rightly conveys quarreling. Water in the semi-arid Negev was precious, and wells were flashpoints for conflict. Isaac names the well Esek ('Contention'), memorializing the strife—a pattern repeated at Sitnah ('Enmity') before peace at Rehoboth.

gloss_terse: Esek, name of a well meaning 'contention' (Genesis 26:20)
gloss_readable: Esek is the name Isaac gave to a well in Genesis 26:20 after the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with his herdsmen, claiming the water belonged to them. The name means 'contention' or 'strife,' commemorating the conflict over water rights. The well's location is unknown today, though it was somewhere in the Negev or northern Sinai. Greek translates the name as Adikia ('Injustice'), interpreting the incident as an unjust seizure. The naming of wells in Genesis often reflects the circumstances of their discovery—Esek stands as a reminder of hostility, contrasted later with Rehoboth ('Broad Places'), where Isaac finds peace.

senses.1: Esek is the well Isaac named in Genesis 26:20 to commemorate the dispute with Gerar's herdsmen: 'because they contended with him.' The name derives directly from the verb for contention or strife. Water sources were vital and contested in the arid regions where Isaac pastured his flocks, and this well became a symbol of conflict. The Greek version renders it Adikia ('Injustice'), highlighting the wrongfulness of the seizure. Esek, along with Sitnah (the next disputed well), contrasts with Rehoboth, where at last 'the Lord has made room for us.' The sequence traces Isaac's journey from conflict to peace.

gloss_terse: Esheq, a personal name in the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:39)
gloss_readable: Esheq is a Benjamite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:39, listed among the descendants of Saul's family line. The name is similar to Esek (the well of contention) and may share the same root, but here it is a personal name. Greek manuscripts render it Asēl or Asek. Beyond this genealogical note, Esheq is otherwise unknown. The Chronicler's genealogies trace Benjamin's prominent families, including the royal line of Saul. Names like Esheq preserve the memory of individuals whose lives are otherwise lost to history but who remain part of the sacred record.

senses.1: Esheq appears in 1 Chronicles 8:39 as a Benjamite, part of the genealogy tracing Saul's descendants. His name may be related to 'Esek' (contention), though it functions here as a personal name without explanation. Greek versions offer Asēl or Asek, reflecting transliteration variance. No narrative accompanies Esheq; he is simply one link in Benjamin's tribal chain. The Chronicler's purpose is to document the continuity of Israel's families, especially Saul's line, which remains part of Benjamin's heritage despite the shift of kingship to David's house. Every name matters in the genealogy of God's people.

gloss_terse: oppression, distress (noun); cry 'I am oppressed!' (Isaiah 38:14)
gloss_readable: Isaiah 38:14 records Hezekiah's prayer during his mortal illness: 'I am oppressed, be my security!' The Hebrew literally says 'oppression to me!' using this rare noun as an exclamation of distress. The word denotes the crushing weight of affliction, the sense of being pressed down by sickness and near-death. Some scholars propose emending to 'my cry' (parallel to 'voice' earlier), but the transmitted text has 'oppression.' Spanish renders 'estoy oprimido' (I am oppressed), capturing Hezekiah's anguish. In the context of terminal illness, oppression is not just external enemies but the internal, existential pressure of mortality.

senses.1: Isaiah 38:14 uses this noun in Hezekiah's lament: 'Oppression to me!' or 'I am oppressed!' The king, facing death, cries out under the crushing weight of illness and divine judgment. The word conveys pressure, being squeezed or hemmed in, with no escape. Some propose textual emendation to 'my cry' for parallelism, but the Hebrew as it stands emphasizes the feeling of oppression—not from human enemies but from disease and divine wrath. Spanish 'estoy oprimido' (I am oppressed) preserves the sense of one burdened beyond his strength. Hezekiah appeals to God as surety, the one who can lift the crushing load.

gloss_terse: twenty (Aramaic indeclinable plural numeral)
gloss_readable: Daniel 6:1 reports that Darius the Mede set 'one hundred and twenty' satraps over his kingdom. This Aramaic numeral is the word for twenty, appearing here as part of a larger number. Aramaic numerals are indeclinable (do not change form for gender or case). The administrative structure described—120 satraps with three presidents over them, including Daniel—sets the stage for the plot against Daniel. The number may be symbolic (12 × 10, representing completeness) or historical. The use of Aramaic reflects the setting: Daniel serving in the imperial court, where Aramaic was the diplomatic language.

senses.1: In Daniel 6:1, this Aramaic numeral forms part of 'one hundred and twenty,' the number of satraps Darius appointed. Aramaic numerals do not inflect, so this is simply 'twenty' as an indeclinable plural. The administrative detail sets the context for Daniel's elevation and subsequent persecution—with so many satraps, there is ample jealousy and intrigue. Whether the number is historical or symbolic (12 × 10), it conveys the vastness of the empire and the high level at which Daniel operates. The Aramaic language signals the book's setting in the cosmopolitan, multilingual world of Babylonian-Persian courts.

gloss_terse: to be smooth, shiny, sleek (possibly from fatness; textually uncertain)
gloss_readable: Jeremiah 5:28 condemns the wicked: 'They have grown fat, they are sleek,' using this verb of uncertain meaning. The traditional interpretation is 'smooth' or 'shiny,' perhaps describing skin that gleams from excess fat and luxury. However, the word is disputed—some propose emending to 'they have grown rich,' which would parallel 'they have grown fat' (v. 27). Spanish uses 'se pusieron lustrosos' (they became glossy/shiny), supporting the smoothness/shininess reading. The context is moral indictment: the wicked prosper materially while oppressing the poor, and their physical appearance reflects their self-indulgence. Whether smooth, shiny, or rich, the image is of comfortable wickedness.

senses.1: Jeremiah 5:28 says the wicked 'have grown fat, they are sleek,' using this verb whose meaning is debated. The traditional sense is 'smooth' or 'shiny'—perhaps their well-fed skin gleams. Some scholars prefer emending to 'rich,' which would better parallel 'fat' (v. 27). Spanish 'lustrosos' (glossy, shiny) supports the transmitted text. The prophet is decrying social injustice: the wicked live in ease and luxury, their prosperity visible in their sleek appearance, while they oppress orphans and the poor. The verb, whatever its precise nuance, paints a picture of self-satisfied affluence built on injustice.

gloss_terse: to think, give thought to (Hithpael Aramaism; consider, be mindful of)
gloss_readable: Jonah 1:6 records the ship's captain pleading with Jonah: 'Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give thought to us, that we may not perish.' This Hithpael verb, an Aramaism, means to think or take thought, to be mindful. It is cognate with Aramaic and Targum usage. The captain hopes that Jonah's God might consider their plight and intervene. The verb parallels Hebrew 'chashav' (to think, reckon). Spanish uses 'se preocupara' (will care/be concerned), capturing the sense of attentive consideration. The pagan sailors fear the storm is divine wrath, and they desperately hope that whichever god is responsible might relent if approached.

senses.1: In Jonah 1:6, the ship's captain urges Jonah to pray: 'Perhaps the god will give thought to us.' This Hithpael verb, borrowed from Aramaic, means to think of, to be mindful, to consider. It parallels Hebrew 'chashav' and appears in Targums with this sense. The captain hopes that divine attention—any god's attention—might avert disaster. Spanish 'se preocupara' (will be concerned) rightly conveys hoping for divine care. The irony is thick: pagan sailors plead for God's mindfulness while the Hebrew prophet sleeps, fleeing from the very God who has already given him too much thought.

gloss_terse: to think, plan, intend (Aramaic verb; passive participle in Daniel 6:3)
gloss_readable: Daniel 6:3 reports that 'the king planned to set him [Daniel] over the whole kingdom,' using this Aramaic verb. The form is strictly a passive participle, meaning 'was thought' or 'was planned,' functioning as a perfect tense. The verb means to think or plan, cognate with Biblical Hebrew and Targum usage (though not found in Syriac). Darius' intention to elevate Daniel triggers the plot by jealous officials to destroy him. Spanish 'pensaba' (he was thinking/planning) captures the deliberative sense. The Aramaic here reflects the language of the imperial court, where Daniel navigates the dangerous politics of high office.

senses.1: Daniel 6:3 uses this Aramaic verb to say the king 'was planning' to elevate Daniel over the entire realm. Technically a passive participle ('was thought,' 'was planned'), it functions as a finite verb. The root means to think or plan, with cognates in Targum and Biblical Hebrew, though Syriac lacks it. The king's favorable intention sets the stage for the conspiracy: Daniel's rivals, seeing he will soon outrank them all, concoct the lions' den scheme. Spanish 'pensaba' (was thinking/planning) rightly conveys the king's deliberate intention. The verb reveals that Daniel's fate hinges on one man's thoughts—yet ultimately, God's plan prevails.

gloss_terse: plate, slab (smooth, shiny object; possibly ivory or metal inlay)
gloss_readable: Song of Solomon 5:14 describes the beloved's body: 'His abdomen is a plate of ivory, encrusted with sapphires.' This rare noun denotes a plate or slab, possibly a smooth, shiny surface. The imagery is of polished ivory, perhaps inlaid with blue stones, evoking both beauty and luxury. The word may derive from a root meaning 'smooth' or 'shiny,' used elsewhere for refined metal. The metaphor compares the beloved's body to precious materials—ivory for its whiteness and smoothness, sapphires for brilliance. The Song's language is extravagant, piling up images of wealth and beauty to convey the lovers' admiration.

senses.1: Song of Solomon 5:14 uses this noun in a metaphor: the beloved's body is 'a plate of ivory.' The term denotes a smooth, flat surface—perhaps a plaque, panel, or slab. The root may relate to smoothness or shininess, as ivory is polished to a lustrous finish. The image evokes luxury: ivory, a rare and costly material, adorned with sapphires. Some see this as describing the torso or belly, smooth and white like carved ivory. The Song's metaphors are sensuous and opulent, and this 'plate of ivory' contributes to the picture of the beloved as a work of art, precious beyond measure.

gloss_terse: thought, thinking (construct noun in Job 12:5)
gloss_readable: Job 12:5 is notoriously difficult: 'In the thought of one at ease there is contempt for calamity.' This rare noun denotes thought or thinking, used here in construct. The verse critiques those who live comfortably and despise the suffering of others, dismissing their misfortune as deserved. The word may be singular or plural (the form is ambiguous), related to a root meaning 'think.' The point is the smug mentality of the prosperous, who in their self-satisfaction have nothing but scorn for disaster—assuming it will never touch them. Job knows better, having been cast from prosperity into ruin.

senses.1: Job 12:5 uses this noun to critique the mindset of the comfortable: 'In the thought of the one at ease there is contempt for misfortune.' The term denotes thinking or mental attitude. Those who live securely, unacquainted with calamity, despise it when they see it in others—judging sufferers as deserving their fate. Job, now a sufferer himself, exposes this callous mentality. The word may be singular or plural (the Hebrew form allows both), but the sense is clear: the prosperous have a thought-pattern that dismisses disaster, because they cannot imagine it happening to them. Job's friends embody this attitude.
